L26: # Spectral isometries of unital $C^{*}$-algebras
L27: 
L28: Matthew J. Colbrook ^{†}^{†}thanks: Corresponding author. Email: m.colbrook@damtp.cam.ac.uk. Affiliation: Department of Applied Mathematics and Theoretical Physics    George Stepaniants ^{†}^{†}thanks: Also at the Courant Institute, New York University, New York, USA. Email: gs852@cam.ac.uk. Affiliation: University of Cambridge, Wilberforce Road, Cambridge CB3 0WA, United Kingdom
L29: ###### Abstract
L30: This paper provides a human digestion of a proof of the spectral isometry conjecture for $C^{*}$-algebras found by GPT-6 Astra. We prove that every unital surjective complex-linear spectral isometry between unital $C^{*}$-algebras is a Jordan isomorphism. Without the assumption that the map preserves the identity, it is a central unitary multiple of a Jordan isomorphism. The main step is to show that an entire one-parameter group of unital spectral isometries consists of algebra automorphisms.
L31: To prove this, we extend the group to the bidual, which splits into finite and properly infinite summands. On the finite part, we use quadratic and cubic trace identities and on the properly infinite part, we apply a structure theorem for maps that preserve square-zero elements. To show that both summands are invariant, we use holomorphic dependence on the parameter together with a uniform resolvent bound, which ensures that self-adjoint elements have images with real spectrum.
L32: We then apply the group theorem to inner automorphisms conjugated by the original spectral isometry. This reduces the problem to the commutative case, where Nagasawa’s theorem completes the proof.
L33: ## 1 Introduction
L34: 
L35: For an element $a$ of a unital complex Banach algebra $A$, let
L36: 
L37:  | $$r_{A}(a)=\max\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma_{A}(a)\}$$  |
L38: denote its spectral radius. A complex-linear map $T:A\to B$ is a spectral isometry if $r_{B}(T(a))=r_{A}(a)$ for every $a\in A$. The spectral isometry conjecture asks whether every unital surjective spectral isometry between unital $C^{*}$-algebras is a Jordan isomorphism; see [【13†11】, Conjecture 4.6] and [【14†9】, Problem 5]. Here, a Jordan isomorphism is a complex-linear bijection that preserves squares.
L39: We prove the conjecture for arbitrary unital $C^{*}$-algebras and the result has been formally verified in Lean [【15†6】].
L40: ###### Theorem 1.1.
L41: 
L42: Let $A$ and $B$ be unital complex $C^{*}$-algebras, and let $T:A\to B$ be a surjective complex-linear map such that
L43: 
L44:  | $$T(1_{A})=1_{B},\qquad r_{B}(T(a))=r_{A}(a)\qquad(a\in A).$$  |
L45: 
L46: Then $T$ is a Jordan isomorphism. In particular,
L47: 
L48:  | $$T(a^{2})=T(a)^{2}\qquad(a\in A).$$  |
L49: Kadison’s theorem identifies unital surjective complex-linear norm isometries between $C^{*}$-algebras as Jordan $*$-isomorphisms [【16†8】, Theorem 7]. Theorem 【17†1.1】 shows that $T$ preserves squares, but not necessarily adjoints. For example, the map $a\mapsto sas^{-1}$, with $s$ invertible, preserves products and spectra but need not preserve adjoints.
L50: The commutative case was already known due to the spectral-radius form of Nagasawa’s theorem [【18†15】, Corollary 2.5] which shows that $T$ is multiplicative, extending the earlier result for uniform algebras [【19†16】]. Previous work also established the conjecture for properly infinite von Neumann algebras [【20†12】] and, more generally, unital $C^{*}$-algebras of real rank zero without tracial states [【21†10】].
L51: Our main contribution is a theorem on entire one-parameter groups of spectral isometries: if $\delta$ is a bounded complex-linear operator on a unital $C^{*}$-algebra and $e^{z\delta}$ is a unital spectral isometry for every $z\in\mathbb{C}$, then $\delta$ is a derivation and every $e^{z\delta}$ is an algebra automorphism (Proposition 【22†4.2】). The proof treats the finite and properly infinite parts of the bidual separately.
L52: A uniform resolvent estimate shows that the extended maps send self-adjoint elements to elements with real spectrum(Lemma 【23†3.2】), while an approximation argument shows that they also preserve square-zero elements.
L53: Using traces on the finite summand, we obtain quadratic and cubic identities from Liouville’s theorem. These identities show that the properly infinite summand is invariant, allowing us to treat the finite part as a quotient. The argument that the tracial identities force preservation of squares comes from Aupetit’s trace method [【24†4】], in the form developed by Mathieu and Schulz [【25†13】].
L54: On the properly infinite summand, we use the weighted Jordan structure of surjective square-zero preservers [【14†9】]. Preservation of real spectra and holomorphy force the central weight to be the identity and the off-diagonal component to vanish. This gives a group of Jordan automorphisms of the bidual; differentiation and Sinclair’s theorem [【26†18】] give the derivation assertion.
L55: To prove Theorem 【17†1.1】, we conjugate inner automorphisms by $T$. Such holomorphic similarity families were used by Costara and Repovš [【27†7】, Lemma 3] and Mathieu and Sourour [【28†14】, Lemma 2.4], under additional assumptions on finite-dimensional representations or quotients. Proposition 【22†4.2】 shows that the generators of these families are derivations for arbitrary unital $C^{*}$-algebras.
L56: For each self-adjoint $h$, we write $T(\{h\}^{\prime\prime})$ as an intersection of kernels of these derivations, so it is a subalgebra. The bicommutant criterion of Mathieu and Sourour [【28†14】, Proposition 3.1] allows us to reduce the proof to the commutative case.
L57: #### AI declaration
L58: 
L59: The proof was found by GPT-6 Astra after a sequence of simple prompts. We then wrote the paper after discussing the proof further with ChatGPT 6 to understand the underlying mechanisms. After we wrote the paper ourselves, ChatGPT 6 was used for minor language editing of the penultimate draft in this stage only.
L60: ## 2 Preliminaries
L61: 
L62: All algebras and linear maps are complex. Identities are denoted by $1$ when the algebra is clear. We identify a $C^{*}$-algebra with its canonical image in its bidual. For a unital algebra $E$, $Z(E)$ denotes its centre and $\operatorname{rad}(E)$ its Jacobson radical. For a compact subset $K$ of $\mathbb{C}$, $\operatorname{conv}K$ denotes its convex hull, which is compact. We omit algebra subscripts on spectral radii and spectra when there is no ambiguity.
L63: Every surjective spectral isometry $T:A\to B$ between $C^{*}$-algebras is injective. Indeed, if $T(a)=0$, then $r(a)=0$ and
L64: 
L65:  | $$r(a+a^{*})=r\bigl(T(a+a^{*})\bigr)=r\bigl(T(a^{*})\bigr)=r(a^{*})=0.$$  |
L66: Since $a+a^{*}$ is self-adjoint, it vanishes. Thus $a$ is skew-adjoint and hence normal, so $\left\lVert a\right\rVert=r(a)=0$. Aupetit’s automatic-continuity theorem [【29†3】], in the form stated in [【14†9】, Theorem 2.1], and the bounded inverse theorem imply that $T$ and $T^{-1}$ are bounded. The case of the zero algebra in Theorem 【17†1.1】 is immediate; henceforth the algebras are nonzero.
L67: We use Kaplansky density, joint strong^{∗} continuity of multiplication on bounded sets, and the decomposition of a von Neumann algebra into finite and properly infinite central summands. A finite von Neumann algebra has a faithful normal centre-valued trace [【30†5】, Theorem III.2.5.7 and Corollary III.2.5.8]. Composing this trace with normal states of the centre gives normal tracial states that separate positive elements.
L68: The strong^{∗} topology on a von Neumann algebra $M$ is generated by the seminorms $x\mapsto\bigl(\varphi(x^{*}x)+\varphi(xx^{*})\bigr)^{1/2}$, where $\varphi\in M_{*}^{+}$.
L69: ###### Lemma 2.1.
L70: 
L71: A bounded weak^{∗}-continuous linear map between von Neumann algebras is strong^{∗}-continuous on norm-bounded sets.
L72: ###### Proof.
L73: 
L74: This follows from Akemann’s continuity theorem [【31†1】, Corollary III.10], first on the unit ball and then by rescaling. The bounded preadjoint maps weakly compact sets to weakly compact sets, giving continuity for the Mackey topologies. These coincide with the strong^{∗} topologies on bounded sets [【31†1】, Theorem II.7]. ∎
L75: The next elementary formula converts spectral information about perturbations into a resolvent bound. For a unital algebra $D$, let $D^{-1}$ denote its group of invertible elements.
L76: ###### Lemma 2.2.
L77: 
L78: If $c$ is invertible in a unital $C^{*}$-algebra $D$, then
L79: 
L80:  | $$\operatorname{dist}(c,D\setminus D^{-1})=\left\lVert c^{-1}\right\rVert^{-1}.$$  |
L81: 
L82: ###### Proof.
L83: 
L84: The Neumann series gives the lower bound. For the reverse bound, let $c=v|c|$ be the polar decomposition of $c$ and let $m=\min\sigma(|c|)=\left\lVert c^{-1}\right\rVert^{-1}.$ The element $v$ is unitary, and $c-mv=v(|c|-m1)$ is noninvertible. Its distance from $c$ is $m$. ∎
L85: ## 3 Passage to the bidual
L86: 
L87: Throughout this section, $U:C\to D$ is a unital bijective spectral isometry between unital $C^{*}$-algebras. We establish two properties of $U^{**}$ used in the next section.
L88: 
L89: ### 3.1 Real spectra and a resolvent estimate
L90: 
L91: Preservation of convex hulls of spectra is due to Mathieu and Schick [【13†11】, Proposition 4.8]. Its short proof will also be useful for the resolvent estimate.
L92: ###### Lemma 3.1.
L93: 
L94: For every $x\in C$,
L95: 
L96:  | $$\operatorname{conv}\sigma_{D}(U(x))=\operatorname{conv}\sigma_{C}(x).$$  |
L97: 
L98: Consequently, $U$ sends self-adjoint elements to elements with real spectrum.
L99: ###### Proof.
L100: 
L101: Unitality and complex linearity give
L102: 
L103:  | $$r_{D}(U(x)-\lambda 1)=r_{C}(x-\lambda 1)\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb{C}).$$  |
L104: 
L105: For a nonempty compact set $K\subset\mathbb{C}$, define $d_{K}(\lambda)=\max_{w\in K}|w-\lambda|$. For every $\theta\in\mathbb{R}$, the support function of $K$ satisfies
L106: 
L107:  | $$\max_{w\in K}\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}w)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\bigl(d_{K}(-te^{i\theta})-t\bigr).$$  |
L108: Thus $d_{K}$ determines $\operatorname{conv}K$. Applying this observation to the two spectra proves the identity. If $x=x^{*}$, its spectrum and hence the spectrum of $U(x)$ lie in $\mathbb{R}$. ∎
L109: 
L110: To pass this conclusion to the bidual, we need uniform control of the resolvents of images of self-adjoint elements.
L111: ###### Lemma 3.2.
L112: 
L113: Let $K=\left\lVert U^{-1}\right\rVert$. For $a=a^{*}\in C$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}$,
L114: 
L115:  | $$\left\lVert(U(a)-\lambda 1)^{-1}\right\rVert\leq\frac{K}{|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|}.$$  |  | (1)
L116: 
L117: Moreover,
L118: 
L119:  | $$a=a^{*}\in C^{**}\quad\rightarrow\quad\sigma_{D^{**}}(U^{**}(a))\subset\mathbb{R}.$$  |  | (2)
L120: ###### Proof.
L121: 
L122: Suppose that $e\in D$ and $\left\lVert e\right\rVert<|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|/K$, and let $h=U^{-1}(e)$. The self-adjoint resolvent estimate and the Neumann series imply that
L123: 
L124:  | $$\sigma_{C}(a+h)\subset\{\zeta\in\mathbb{C}:|\operatorname{Im}\zeta|\leq\left\lVert h\right\rVert\}.$$  |
L125: This strip is convex and does not contain $\lambda$. Lemma 【32†3.1】 therefore shows that $U(a)+e-\lambda 1$ is invertible. Every noninvertible element is consequently at distance at least $|\operatorname{Im}\lambda|/K$ from $U(a)-\lambda 1$. Lemma 【33†2.2】 gives (【34†1】).
